anchorChartsIntro: Start with the seven Midterm focus skills. Each chart has a poster, a how-to guide, five worked examples, and a quick check. The supporting charts after them cover drama, text evidence, and vocabulary in context. These are original study guides that supplement your classroom charts.

anchorCharts.name: Author's Purpose
anchorCharts.body: The author's purpose is the main reason a text was written. Most texts persuade, inform, or entertain (P.I.E.); some also explain how or why, or describe so you can picture something. Look at the whole text, not one sentence, and ask: What does the author want me to think, know, or feel?

guide.label: Persuade · 說服
guide.text: Convince the reader to believe or do something. Clues: an opinion, reasons, evidence, words like should, must, best, never.

guide.label: Inform · 告知
guide.text: Teach facts about a real topic. Clues: facts, numbers, dates, headings, diagrams, captions.

guide.label: Entertain · 娛樂
guide.text: Tell a story or share something fun or exciting. Clues: characters, a problem, dialogue, humor, suspense. Stories, plays, and most poems.

guide.label: Explain · 說明
guide.text: Show how something works or why it happens, often in steps or cause-and-effect order. A special kind of informing.

guide.label: Describe · 描寫
guide.text: Help the reader picture a person, place, or thing with sensory details (see, hear, smell, touch, taste).

steps: Preview: genre, title, headings, pictures. A play or poem is usually written to entertain; an article usually informs.
Read and collect clues: opinions and reasons, facts and numbers, or characters and events.
Name ONE main purpose and support it with two details from the text.
Ask what else the author does: an article can also persuade at the end; a story can also teach a lesson.
anchorCharts.tip: A text can have more than one purpose. Choose the MAIN one. A persuasive text still uses facts, and a story with a few facts is still mainly written to entertain.
ex:
“Every class should plant a spring garden. Gardens teach science, give us fresh food, and make the school beautiful. Ask your principal today!”
Persuade. An opinion (“should”), three reasons, and a call to action (“Ask your principal today!”).

“A seed needs three things to germinate: water, air, and the right temperature. When water soaks through the seed coat, the tiny plant inside begins to grow.”
Inform / explain. Facts about a real process, told in cause-and-effect order, with no opinion.

“The airship dropped twenty feet in one second. Kate grabbed the rail and laughed. ‘Is that all you’ve got, storm?’”
Entertain. A character, a dangerous problem, dialogue, and suspense.

“The old garden was a tangle of gray branches, damp brown leaves, and vines that clung to the walls like cold fingers.”
Describe. Sight and touch details and a simile help you picture the setting; nothing is argued or taught.

An article tells how airships were invented, gives dates and inventors, then ends: “We should build airships again because they use less fuel than planes.”
Main purpose: inform; second purpose: persuade. Most of the text gives facts; only the ending gives an opinion with a reason.

check.question: “Three Ways to Keep Your Seedlings Alive: First, water the soil when the top feels dry. Next, place the pot in a sunny window. Finally, turn the pot every day so the stems grow straight.” What is the author’s main purpose?
check.answer: To explain / inform: it teaches how to care for seedlings in steps (first, next, finally). There is no story and no opinion to argue.

anchorCharts.name: Text Structure
anchorCharts.body: Text structure is the way an author organizes information. Nonfiction often uses one of five structures. Signal words are clues, but the real test is how the ideas connect. Stories, plays, and poems have structures too: chapters, scenes, and stanzas fit together to build the whole work (RL.5.5).

guide.label: Description
guide.text: A topic and its details or features. Signal words: for example, such as, including, also, in addition.

guide.label: Sequence / Chronological
guide.text: Events or steps in time order. Signal words: first, next, then, after, finally, dates and times.

guide.label: Compare & Contrast
guide.text: How two things are alike and different. Signal words: both, similarly, like, however, but, unlike, on the other hand.

guide.label: Cause & Effect
guide.text: Why something happens (cause) and what happens as a result (effect). Signal words: because, so, as a result, therefore, since.

guide.label: Problem & Solution
guide.text: A problem is described, then one or more ways to solve it. Signal words: problem, challenge, solve, solution, one answer is.

guide.label: Chapters · Scenes · Stanzas
guide.text: Literary structure: chapters build a novel, scenes build a play, stanzas build a poem. Each part adds something: a new event, a change in setting, or a new idea.

steps: Find the topic. Then ask: what is the author mostly doing with it?
Circle signal words, but check that they match the whole passage, not just one sentence.
Sketch a quick organizer: a web, a timeline, a Venn diagram, cause → effect arrows, or problem → solution boxes.
Explain WHY the author chose that structure: it helps the reader follow steps, compare, or understand a result.
anchorCharts.tip: One “because” does not make a whole passage cause and effect. Choose the structure that organizes MOST of the text.
ex:
“First, soak the bean seeds overnight. Next, plant them two centimeters deep. After about a week, a curled shoot pushes up through the soil.”
Sequence. Steps in time order: first, next, after about a week.

“Both airships and airplanes carry passengers. However, an airship floats because it is filled with a light gas, while an airplane needs wings and speed to stay up.”
Compare & contrast. “Both” shows a likeness; “however” and “while” show differences.

“Because the spring rains came late, the soil stayed dry. As a result, many seeds did not sprout until May.”
Cause & effect. Late rain (cause) → dry soil → late sprouting (effects).

“Rabbits kept eating the school’s lettuce. The students solved the problem by building a fence of chicken wire around the beds.”
Problem & solution. A problem (rabbits) is followed by how it was fixed (a fence).

A play has three scenes: Scene 1, Mary finds a locked garden; Scene 2, she discovers the key; Scene 3, the garden blooms.
Scenes as structure. Each scene moves the plot forward: problem → discovery → resolution (RL.5.5).

check.question: “Hot-air balloons and airships both float because they are lighter than the air around them. Unlike a balloon, however, an airship has engines and can be steered.” Which structure is this?
check.answer: Compare and contrast: “both” shows how they are alike, and “unlike” and “however” show how they are different.

anchorCharts.name: Theme
anchorCharts.body: The theme is the message or life lesson of a story, play, or poem. It is written as a full sentence that could be true for many people, not just one character. Find it by watching how characters respond to challenges and what they learn, or, in a poem, how the speaker reflects on a topic (RL.5.2).

guide.label: Topic ≠ Theme
guide.text: A topic is one or two words (courage, friendship). A theme is a full sentence about that topic: “Courage means acting even when you are afraid.”

guide.label: Challenge
guide.text: What problem does the main character face?

guide.label: Response
guide.text: How does the character respond? What choices does he or she make?

guide.label: Outcome & Change
guide.text: What happens because of those choices? How has the character changed by the end?

guide.label: Lesson
guide.text: What does the character learn, and what can the reader learn too? Turn it into a sentence that works for anyone.

steps: Name the topic in one or two words.
Track the challenge → response → outcome → change.
Write the theme as a full sentence without character names (use people, we, or you).
Prove it with two details from the beginning AND the end of the text.
anchorCharts.tip: Don’t retell the plot (“Mary found a garden”) and don’t write only a topic (“nature”). A theme also isn’t one character’s action; it is a lesson for everyone.
ex:
A lonely, angry girl secretly cares for a dying garden. As the plants grow, she makes friends and becomes kind.
Theme: Caring for something outside yourself can help you grow too. Topic: growth, friendship.

A cabin boy is afraid of heights, but when a stranger’s balloon is in trouble, he climbs out to help and saves the man.
Theme: Courage means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.

A boy tries to write a poem for a contest. Each version fails, but he keeps adding lines until it becomes his best work.
Theme: Mistakes and hard work are part of creating something good.

Poem: the speaker watches a frozen pond, then sees the first green buds and hears returning birds in spring.
Theme (speaker reflects): After hard times, hope and new beginnings always return.

Two friends argue over who will lead a class play. The show goes badly until they agree to share the job.
Theme: People can achieve more by working together than by competing.

check.question: Leo laughs at his grandmother’s old-fashioned stories. When he gets lost on a hike, he remembers her advice about following the stream downhill, and he finds his way home. Write the theme, not the topic.
check.answer: Sample: “The wisdom of older people can be valuable, even if it seems old-fashioned.” The topic is respect or wisdom; the theme is the full lesson Leo learns.

anchorCharts.name: Figurative Language
anchorCharts.body: Figurative language uses words in an unusual way to create a picture or feeling. The words do NOT mean exactly what they say (that would be literal). For each example: name it → explain what it really means → tell why the author used it (RL.5.4, L.5.5).

guide.label: Simile
guide.text: Compares two unlike things using like or as. “The airship floated like a silver whale.”

guide.label: Metaphor
guide.text: Compares by saying one thing IS another, without like or as. “The garden was a sleeping giant.”

guide.label: Personification
guide.text: Gives human actions or feelings to an animal, object, or idea. “The wind tugged at my sleeve.”

guide.label: Hyperbole
guide.text: A huge exaggeration for effect, not meant to be believed. “I’ve told you a million times!”

guide.label: Idiom
guide.text: A saying whose meaning can’t be figured out from the words. “Break a leg!” means “Good luck!”

guide.label: Sound devices
guide.text: Alliteration repeats beginning sounds (“silent, silver sky”). Onomatopoeia names a sound (buzz, creak, whoosh).

steps: Notice a phrase that can’t be literally true.
Name the type: look for like/as (simile), is/was (metaphor), human actions (personification), exaggeration (hyperbole), or a saying (idiom).
Explain the real meaning in plain words.
Explain the effect: what does it make you picture or feel?
anchorCharts.tip: Not every “like” is a simile: “I like apples” compares nothing. A simile compares two DIFFERENT kinds of things: “Her voice was like a bell.”
ex:
“The clouds swallowed the airship whole.”
Personification / metaphor. Clouds can’t swallow; it means the ship disappeared completely into thick clouds. It makes the clouds seem huge and dangerous.

“The tendrils clung to the wall like tiny green hands.”
Simile (uses like). The curly stems hold on tightly, the way small hands would grip.

“Colin’s room was a prison.”
Metaphor. The room is not a real prison; it shows that Colin feels trapped and lonely there.

“This suitcase weighs a ton!”
Hyperbole. It doesn’t really weigh 1,000 kg; the speaker means it is very heavy and shows how tired he is.

“Mom said I was skating on thin ice when I came home late.”
Idiom. “Skating on thin ice” means being close to getting in trouble; it has nothing to do with real ice.

check.question: “The old floorboards groaned as we tiptoed through the silent house.” Name the figurative language and explain its effect.
check.answer: Personification: floorboards can’t groan like a person, so the creaking sounds tired and spooky. It builds a nervous, mysterious mood.

anchorCharts.name: Character
anchorCharts.body: Authors reveal characters directly (the narrator tells you: “Mary was rude”) and indirectly (you infer from what the character does and says). Use the S.T.E.A.L. clues to describe a character’s traits, feelings, motivations, and changes, and compare characters using specific details (RL.5.3).

guide.label: S · Speech
guide.text: What does the character say, and how? (shouts, whispers, teases)

guide.label: T · Thoughts
guide.text: What does the character think, wish, or worry about?

guide.label: E · Effect on others
guide.text: How do other characters react to him or her? Do they trust, fear, or avoid this person?

guide.label: A · Actions
guide.text: What does the character do, especially when facing a problem?

guide.label: L · Looks
guide.text: What does the character look like? Clothes, face, and body language (a frown, slumped shoulders).

guide.label: Trait · Feeling · Motivation
guide.text: Trait = what someone is like most of the time (stubborn, loyal). Feeling = an emotion right now (nervous). Motivation = why the character acts (wants a friend, wants to be brave).

steps: Collect S.T.E.A.L. clues from the text.
Infer a trait word that fits several clues (curious, not just “nice”).
Track change: what is the character like at the beginning and at the end, and what caused the change?
To compare two characters, put the same kind of clue side by side: how each one reacts to the same problem.
anchorCharts.tip: A feeling is not a trait. Someone who is angry once isn’t an angry person. A trait shows up again and again in the character’s actions and words.
ex:
“Mary stamped her foot. ‘I won’t go! You can’t make me!’”
Trait: stubborn / spoiled. Clues: Speech (“You can’t make me”) and Action (stamped her foot).

“Matt glanced at the dark sky, then climbed the ladder anyway, gripping each rung until his knuckles were white.”
Feeling: afraid. Trait: brave. White knuckles show fear (Looks); climbing anyway shows courage (Action).

“Whenever Dickon walked into the garden, the robin flew down to his shoulder and the other children stopped arguing.”
Trait: gentle and calming. Clue: Effect on others; animals and people relax around him.

Beginning: Colin refuses to leave his bed. Ending: he walks through the garden and laughs with his friends.
Character change: from fearful and hopeless to confident and hopeful, caused by fresh air and friendship.

Compare: when the storm hits, Nell rushes to tie down the cover, but Owen hides in the cabin and pretends to sleep.
Contrast (RL.5.3): both face the same problem; Nell is responsible and brave, while Owen avoids danger.

check.question: “Ava handed her last cookie to the new student, then quietly sat back down without saying a word about it.” What trait does this show, and which S.T.E.A.L. clues prove it?
check.answer: Generous and modest. Action: she gives away her last cookie. Speech: she says nothing about it, so she isn’t showing off.

anchorCharts.name: Literary Elements
anchorCharts.body: Literary elements are the parts every story or play is built from: characters, setting, conflict, plot, and the narrator’s point of view. Genre changes how these elements are used. That is the Module 2 big question: How does genre affect the way a story is told?

guide.label: Characters
guide.text: The people or animals in the story. The main character (protagonist) faces the problem; an antagonist works against him or her.

guide.label: Setting
guide.text: Where and when the story happens. A setting can cause the problem (a storm) or create a mood (a dark, quiet house).

guide.label: Conflict
guide.text: The main problem. Character vs. character, vs. nature, vs. society, or vs. self (an inner struggle).

guide.label: Plot
guide.text: Exposition (introduce characters and setting) → rising action → climax (turning point) → falling action → resolution.

guide.label: Point of View
guide.text: Who tells the story. First person (I, we: a character tells it) or third person (he, she, they: an outside narrator).

guide.label: Genre
guide.text: Fantasy/adventure (exciting action, unusual worlds), realistic fiction, myth, drama (dialogue and stage directions), poetry. Each genre tells a story in a different way.

steps: Name the main character and the setting (time and place).
Identify the conflict and its type.
Put the key events on a plot mountain and mark the climax.
Explain how the resolution settles the conflict and how the genre shaped the telling.
anchorCharts.tip: The climax is the TURNING POINT where the conflict is decided, not just the loudest moment. Everything after it is falling action and resolution.
ex:
“High above the clouds in 1910, the airship Aurora hummed through the night.”
Setting: in the sky, at night, in 1910. It suggests an adventure far from help.

“Nell had to choose: tell the captain she broke the compass, or let the cook take the blame.”
Conflict: character vs. self. Nell struggles with an inner choice about honesty.

“The storm tore the sail loose, and the ship began to spin toward the sea.”
Conflict: character vs. nature. The storm is the force the characters must fight.

Mary finds a key (rising action), opens the hidden door (climax: the turning point), and plants seeds with Dickon (falling action); by summer the garden is alive (resolution).
Plot mapped onto the plot mountain.

“I gripped the rail and stared down at the waves.” vs. “Matt gripped the rail and stared down at the waves.”
Point of view: the first uses I (first person); the second uses Matt (third person).

check.question: Sam is too shy to sing in the school show. He practices in front of his dog every night. On show night his hands shake, but he steps onto the stage and sings his solo. Afterward, he signs up for choir. Which event is the climax, and what type of conflict is it?
check.answer: Climax: Sam steps onto the stage and sings. That is the turning point where his problem is decided. Conflict: character vs. self, because his struggle is with his own shyness. Signing up for choir is the resolution.

anchorCharts.name: Elements of Poetry
anchorCharts.body: A poem is built from lines grouped into stanzas. Poets use sound (rhyme, rhythm, repetition) and images (sensory and figurative language) to share a feeling or idea. The speaker is the voice in the poem; it is not always the poet. Stanzas fit together to build the poem’s meaning (RL.5.5).

guide.label: Line & Stanza
guide.text: A line is one row of words. A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in a poem.

guide.label: Rhyme & Rhyme Scheme
guide.text: Rhyme: words that end with the same sound (night/light). Rhyme scheme: the pattern of rhymes at line ends, labeled with letters (AABB, ABAB).

guide.label: Rhythm & Meter
guide.text: Rhythm is the beat you hear when you read aloud. Meter is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

guide.label: Repetition & Refrain
guide.text: Repetition repeats words or sounds for emphasis. A refrain is a line or stanza repeated regularly, like a song’s chorus.

guide.label: Imagery & Figurative Language
guide.text: Words that appeal to the five senses, plus simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration, and onomatopoeia.

guide.label: Speaker · Form
guide.text: The speaker is the voice telling the poem. Forms include rhyming poems, free verse (no regular rhyme or meter), narrative poems (tell a story), and limericks.

steps: Read the poem aloud twice and listen for the beat and the rhymes.
Count the stanzas and lines; label the rhyme scheme with letters.
Mark repeated words or a refrain and ask why they are repeated.
Find the strongest images; decide what the speaker feels and what the poem’s theme is.
anchorCharts.tip: Label the rhyme scheme by SOUND, not spelling: “through” and “blue” rhyme, but “cough” and “dough” do not. A new sound always gets the next letter.
ex:
“The rain begins to fall (A) / Upon the garden wall (A) / The seeds wake up below (B) / And start to stretch and grow (B)”
Rhyme scheme: AABB. Lines 1-2 rhyme (fall/wall); lines 3-4 rhyme (below/grow).

“The moon’s a lamp so bright (A) / That hangs above the town (B) / It shines all through the night (A) / Until the sun comes down (B)”
ABAB rhyme scheme (bright/night, town/down), and a metaphor: the moon IS a lamp.

Every stanza of a poem ends with “And still the poem goes on and on.”
Refrain. The repeated line ties the stanzas together and makes the poem feel endless.

“Splash! Drip, drip. The puddles plop / as raindrops tap the tin roof top.”
Onomatopoeia (splash, drip, plop, tap) creates the sound of rain; the rhyme plop/top gives it a bouncy rhythm.

“I stand by the window. / Snow falls without a sound. / I wait for my father’s car.”
Free verse (no rhyme or set beat). The speaker is a child waiting; the quiet imagery shows loneliness and hope.

check.question: “A cat sat on a mat, (A) / Wearing a tiny hat. (?) / It purred a happy tune, (?) / And napped all afternoon. (?)” Write the rhyme scheme.
check.answer: AABB: mat/hat share the A sound; tune/afternoon share a new B sound.

anchorCharts.name: Elements of Drama
anchorCharts.body: A drama, or play, is a story written to be performed. Readers learn almost everything through dialogue and stage directions instead of a narrator.

guide.label: Cast of characters
guide.text: The list at the beginning that names each character and often describes them.

guide.label: Dialogue
guide.text: The words the characters speak. Each line begins with the speaker’s name, with no quotation marks.

guide.label: Stage directions
guide.text: Italic words, usually in parentheses, that tell actors how to move or speak and describe the setting, sound, and lighting.

guide.label: Scenes and acts
guide.text: Plays are divided into scenes (and sometimes acts). A new scene often means a change in time or place.

guide.label: Setting description
guide.text: Stage directions at the start of a scene that describe the time, place, and set.

steps: Read the cast list to learn who is who.
Read the stage directions carefully; they show feelings and actions the dialogue does not say.
Compare scenes to see how time, place, and characters change.
anchorCharts.tip: Stage directions are not spoken aloud. A character’s feelings may be shown only in a direction like (with contempt) or (eyes shining).
ex: In The Garden Behind the Wall, (with contempt) tells the actor playing Rosa to say “This whole place is dead” scornfully.
Scene 1 is early spring with dead vines; Scene 2 is six weeks later with roses on the wall. The scene change shows time passing and the garden’s recovery.

check.question: “SAM: (slamming the door) Fine. I don’t care anyway.” What does the stage direction suggest that the words alone do not?
check.answer: Slamming the door shows Sam is angry or upset, so “I don’t care” probably is not true. The direction reveals his real feelings.

anchorCharts.name: Text Evidence
anchorCharts.body: Text evidence is a specific detail from the text that supports an answer. You can quote exactly or paraphrase accurately.

guide.label: Answer
guide.text: Make a clear statement that answers the question.

guide.label: Evidence
guide.text: Choose a relevant action, fact, line, or stage direction. Name the paragraph, scene, or stanza when helpful.

guide.label: Explain
guide.text: Show how the detail supports your answer: “This shows … because …”.

steps: Underline the important words in the question.
Return to the text and choose the strongest matching detail.
Connect the evidence to your answer in your own words.
anchorCharts.tip: In “Which sentence best supports…” questions, several choices may be true. Pick the one that PROVES the idea in the question, not just one that is about the same topic.
ex: Answer: Grandma Ines has changed. Evidence: “I have been sitting still for far too long. Bring me that packet of seeds.” Explanation: she was always in her chair, and now she joins the work.
To show that dormancy protects a seed, use “the next hard frost would kill the tender young plant,” not a sentence that only defines dormancy.

check.question: Question: Is Captain Osei calm? Text: “The captain did not panic. ‘Every hand I have is holding this ship steady,’ he said.” Write an answer with evidence.
check.answer: Yes, Captain Osei is calm. The text says he “did not panic,” and he explains the situation clearly instead of shouting, even in a storm.

anchorCharts.name: Vocabulary in Context
anchorCharts.body: Use nearby words, sentences, and events to infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word. Then test that meaning in the sentence.

guide.label: Definition or restatement
guide.text: “A seed begins to grow, or germinate…” The words after “or” give the meaning.

guide.label: Example
guide.text: “A plant without enough nitrogen often develops pale yellow leaves.” The example explains deficiency as a lack.

guide.label: Contrast
guide.text: “The vines are matted on top, but look underneath.” The contrast hints at a thick, tangled surface.

guide.label: Situation
guide.text: Nell grips the rail at the first post before moving on. Her actions explain hesitated: paused because she was unsure or afraid.

steps: Read before and after the unfamiliar word.
Find a clue and suggest a meaning that fits the context.
Substitute your meaning and reread; check word parts if useful.
anchorCharts.tip: Choose the meaning used in THIS text. “Project” can mean a school assignment or to throw a light or voice outward.
ex: In How a Seed Wakes Up, seeds planted too densely “crowd one another.” The clue shows densely means packed closely together.
“A seed begins to grow… only when conditions are favorable” and then lists what it needs. Favorable means helpful or just right.

check.question: “The kitten was restless; it paced, pawed at the door, and would not settle on its blanket.” What does restless mean, and what is the clue?
check.answer: Restless means unable to stay still or relax. Pacing, pawing, and refusing to settle all show it cannot rest.

passages.title: Storm over the Kestrel
passages.body: Original practice story written in the style of an adventure novel. Paragraphs are numbered. 1 The airship Kestrel hummed over the dark ocean like a giant bee that had lost its way home. From the small round porthole beside her bunk, Nell Varga could see nothing below but black water and, now and then, the white scribble of a wave. She was twelve years old and the youngest crew member aboard, and her job was simple: polish the brass, carry messages, and stay out of the way. 2 Tonight she was restless. The wind had been growling at the hull since supper, and the floor kept tilting beneath her feet. Something about the sky felt wrong, as if the clouds were holding their breath. 3 A loud crack split the air. Nell pressed her face to the glass. Far back along the outer catwalk, a dark shape flapped and twisted in the wind. It was the canvas cover over the cargo hold, and one of its fastenings had snapped. If the cover tore away, rain would pour onto the contents of the hold: three hundred crates of medicine bound for the island hospital at Port Ivy. 4 Nell ran to the bridge. Captain Osei stood at the wheel, his watchful eyes fixed on the storm ahead. "The cargo cover is loose!" she gasped. 5 The captain did not panic. "Every hand I have is holding this ship steady," he said. "Mr. Lund will go as soon as he can be spared." 6 "There isn't time," Nell said. "I'm small. I can clip onto the safety line." 7 For a long moment, the captain studied her. Then he nodded once. "Clip on, keep low, and come back the instant I call. That is an order." 8 The catwalk was a narrow ribbon of metal stretched along the side of the ship. The wind seized Nell's jacket and tried to drag her into the sky. Her heart hammered. At the first post she hesitated, gripping the rail so tightly that her knuckles turned white. Below her, the ocean waited like an open mouth. 9 She thought of the hospital at Port Ivy and of the children who would wake up tomorrow needing the medicine in those crates. She took one breath, then another, and inched forward. 10 The loose cover cracked like a whip above her head. On her first attempt to grab its corner, the canvas jerked free and slapped her shoulder. On her second, she caught it and pulled with all her weight. Rain stung her face. Her arms burned. At last she looped the rope through the iron ring, tied the knot her father had taught her, and tugged it tight. The cover lay flat and still. 11 When Nell stumbled back onto the bridge, soaked and shaking, the captain did not scold her. He handed her a towel and a cup of warm tea. "Tomorrow," he said, "you'll learn to tie the storm knots properly. A crew is only as strong as its smallest member." 12 Through the porthole, the first gray light of morning was creeping over the clouds. Nell smiled. For the first time since she had come aboard, she felt that the Kestrel truly belonged to her, too.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the setting of the story?
choices: A busy island hospital on a sunny morning
A ship's cargo hold during a calm night at sea
An airship flying over the ocean at night during a storm
A harbor where an airship is being repaired

questions.q: What is the main conflict in the story?
choices: Nell must secure the loose cargo cover before the storm ruins the medicine.
Nell and Captain Osei argue about who should steer the airship.
Mr. Lund refuses to help Nell polish the brass.
The hospital at Port Ivy does not want the medicine.

questions.q: Which event is the climax of the story?

passages.title: The Garden Behind the Wall
passages.body: Original practice play. Read the cast list and the stage directions (in italics and parentheses) carefully. The Garden Behind the Wall A Play in Two Scenes CAST OF CHARACTERS ROSA, an eleven-year-old girl who has just moved in with her grandmother GRANDMA INES, Rosa's grandmother, who rarely leaves her chair by the window THEO, a boy from next door who loves growing things SCENE 1 (Early spring. A yard behind an old stone house. Dead brown vines cover a high wall. A rusty gate hangs open. ROSA kicks at a pile of dry leaves.) ROSA: (with contempt) This whole place is dead. Even the weeds have given up. THEO: (peering over the wall) It isn't dead. It's sleeping. ROSA: (startled, spinning around) Who are you? Were you spying on me? THEO: I'm Theo. I live next door. (He climbs over the wall and kneels beside it. He pulls back a clump of tangled stems.) See? The vines are matted on top, but look underneath. ROSA: (leaning closer, curious in spite of herself) It's green. There's a tiny green tendril curling around the stem! THEO: Your grandpa planted this garden. After he died, nobody touched it for three years. ROSA: (quietly) Grandma never talks about him. She just sits by the window all day. THEO: Maybe the garden could talk for her. (ROSA hesitates. Then she picks up a rusty rake leaning against the gate and begins to pull away the dead leaves. Lights fade.) SCENE 2 (Six weeks later. The same yard, now cleared. Rows of young plants line the beds. Pink roses climb the wall. Birds sing. ROSA and THEO are digging. GRANDMA INES appears in the doorway, leaning on a cane.) GRANDMA INES: (in a shaky voice) What have you done? ROSA: (dropping her trowel, nervous) I'm sorry, Grandma. I should have asked. We found Grandpa's notebook in the shed. He scrawled the name of every plant on the first page, so we knew what to look for. (GRANDMA INES walks slowly down the steps. She touches a rose as if it were made of glass.) GRANDMA INES: He planted these the year your mother was born. I thought they had died with him. THEO: They only needed someone to wake them up. GRANDMA INES: (turning to ROSA, her eyes shining) When you came here, you were as gray as this yard. Now look at you. You have dirt on your nose and sunshine in your face. ROSA: (laughing and wiping her nose) Will you help us, Grandma? You must know where everything belongs. GRANDMA INES: (lowering herself onto the garden bench and reaching for a trowel) I have been sitting still for far too long. Bring me that packet of seeds. (The three work side by side as the lights slowly grow brighter. Curtain.)

passages.title: How a Seed Wakes Up
passages.body: An informational article. Paragraphs are numbered. How a Seed Wakes Up 1 All winter long, a seed can lie in the cold ground looking as lifeless as a pebble. Yet inside its hard coat, a tiny plant is waiting. When the season changes, that plant will awaken and push its way toward the light. How does a seed know when it is time to grow? The answer lies in a series of signals from its surroundings. Waiting for the Right Moment 2 A seed has three main parts. The seed coat is a tough outer layer that protects everything inside. The embryo is the baby plant. The endosperm, or stored food, gives the embryo energy until it can make its own. These parts allow a seed to survive for months, or even years, without growing at all. This resting state is called dormancy. 3 Dormancy protects the seed. If a seed sprouted during a warm week in December, the next hard frost would kill the tender young plant. Therefore, many seeds will not grow until they have gone through a long stretch of cold. The cold works like a calendar, telling the seed that winter has truly passed. The Signals of Spring 4 A seed begins to grow, or germinate, only when conditions are favorable. It needs three things: water, oxygen, and the right temperature. In spring, melting snow and rain soak the soil. Because the seed coat absorbs this water, the seed swells and its coat splits open. At the same time, warmer soil speeds up the chemical changes inside the seed. From Seed to Seedling 5 Germination follows a predictable order. First, the root pushes downward. It anchors the plant and begins drawing water from the soil. Next, a shoot curls upward toward the surface. Once the shoot breaks through the soil, its first leaves unfold. Finally, the leaves begin to use sunlight to make food, a process called photosynthesis. The stored food is used up, and the seedling now feeds itself. When Things Go Wrong 6 Not every seed succeeds. If seeds are planted too densely, the seedlings crowd one another and compete for water and light, so many grow weak and thin. A seedling may also suffer from a deficiency of nutrients. For example, a plant without enough nitrogen often develops pale yellow leaves. Gardeners prevent these problems by spacing seeds carefully and enriching the soil with compost. 7 It is reasonable to think of spring as one sudden change, but for a seed, it is a careful chain of events. Each step depends on the one before it. The next time you notice green shoots poking through the soil, remember that each one waited, tested its world, and began at exactly the right moment.

passages.body: Three original poems. Read each poem aloud to hear its rhythm and sounds. Lines in italics are a refrain. Poem 1: The Ditty That Wouldn't Quit On Monday, Bartholomew learned a new ditty, A silly old tune about Pete and his kitty. He hummed it at breakfast, he hummed it at nine, He hummed it while waiting in the lunchroom line. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! His teacher said, "Bart, could you hush for a while?" His sister just groaned with a sour little smile. The dog howled along with a long, wobbly "Woo!" The kettle went whistling. It sang the song, too! Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! He tried to restrain it; he pressed his lips tight, But it buzzed in his bones like a bee in the night. He scrawled it on paper and buried it deep, But it climbed out and sang to him all through his sleep. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! So now that you've read it, I'm sorry to say, You'll be humming it, too, for the rest of the day. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! Poem 2: What the Garden Knows Under the frost, the garden is a closed book no one has learned to read. Then April arrives, soft-footed, knocking on the door of every seed. A tendril unrolls like a question mark, asking the sky, Is it time? The robins answer. The rain answers. The sun leans close and whispers, Yes. Poem 3: Spring Rain Pitter, patter, on the pane, Drip and drop and splash and spill, Here's the music of the rain Dancing down the windowsill. Every puddle is a drum, Every gutter hums along. Come and listen, children, come! Spring is singing her first song.

passages.title: Author's Purpose and Text Structure Practice
passages.body: Practice set. Read each short excerpt, then decide the author's purpose and how the text is organized. Author's purpose: persuade (convince), inform or explain (teach facts, show how or why), entertain (tell a story or poem). Text structures: description, sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution. Excerpt 1. Every family should grow at least one plant on a windowsill. Caring for a plant teaches children patience and responsibility. Fresh herbs make meals taste better. Best of all, a pot of soil and a packet of seeds cost less than a movie ticket. Start your window garden this weekend! Excerpt 2. Pea plants climb by using tendrils, thin curling threads that wrap around anything they touch. A single tendril can coil around a string in less than an hour. Tendrils help the plant lift its leaves toward the sunlight without growing a thick, heavy stem. Excerpt 3. Gus the squirrel had a plan. Every night he crept into Mrs. Patel's flowerbed, dug up one tulip bulb, and buried it in the neighbor's yard. By April, the neighbor had a mysterious row of red tulips, and Mrs. Patel had a very bare garden and a very puzzled face. Excerpt 4. To grow a bean in a jar, first fold a wet paper towel and press it against the inside of a clear jar. Next, slide a bean between the towel and the glass. Then place the jar in a warm, sunny spot. After about five days, you will witness a root poking out. Finally, watch for the first green leaves. Excerpt 5. Hot-air balloons and airships both float because they are lighter than the air around them. However, a hot-air balloon can only drift wherever the wind blows it. An airship, unlike a balloon, has engines and a rudder, so a pilot can steer it in any direction. Excerpt 6. Hydrogen is the lightest gas, but it catches fire very easily. As a result, early airships that were filled with hydrogen were dangerous to fly. For this reason, modern airships are filled with helium, a gas that does not burn. Excerpt 7. Every recess, students ran straight through the school garden and trampled the young plants. The garden club decided to take action for their spring project. They built a low wooden fence, painted bright signs, and made a stone path around the beds. Within a week, the plants were growing safely again. Excerpt 8. In September 1783, two French brothers sent a hot-air balloon into the sky carrying a sheep, a duck, and a rooster. The animals landed safely about eight minutes later. Two months after that, in November, two men made the first free flight in one of the brothers' balloons and drifted over Paris for about twenty-five minutes.

passages.title: Finding Prince Deming (Week 1 HW)
passages.body: Module 2 Week 1 homework passage (HW3). Paragraphs are numbered. 1 "Hartwig!" Old King Bo called. He had a puzzling problem and needed his quick-witted advisor to help him untangle it. 2 "What is it, Your Majesty?" asked Hartwig as he hurried into the throne room. 3 "Two young men have come to the castle, both claiming to be Prince Deming from the North Forest. As you know, the true Prince Deming will eventually be crowned king and will start studying with me tomorrow. How will I tell which is the true prince and which is an imposter, or faker, who is pretending to be the prince?" 4 "First, tell me about them," Hartwig said. 5 "This morning, both men arrived dressed in dusty cloaks," King Bo began. "They had traveled from the same direction, and their faces had tired lines across them." 6 "Did you speak with them separately?" Hartwig asked. 7 "Yes, I asked each of them about the North Forest, and both said the pine trees there are so tall they look like prickly green mountains. They gave the same answers to every question I asked. Each claimed he'd met the other prince while traveling and that the other had followed him to the castle hoping to steal his place." He groaned in dismay. "How will I know which one to trust with my secrets?" 8 After thinking briefly, Hartwig explained his idea to the king, who nodded in approval. 9 That afternoon, Hartwig commanded the two princes to follow him across the drawbridge and down a grassy hill to a patch of black soil. Then Hartwig took some little seeds from a silky pouch and whispered in a mysterious voice, "Ebba-ebba-ebba-bee." 10 The princes stared at Hartwig, their eyes the size of dinner plates. They knew Hartwig had amazing powers and almost expected the seeds to magically change into a terrifying creature. 11 Facing them with a hint of a smile, Hartwig handed each prince a seed. "You must each plant one seed. In the morning, there will be a purple flower growing that will reveal the true Prince Deming." 12 So he does use magic to find his answers, Prince One thought as he nervously dropped a seed into the earth. 13 Prince Two planted his seed and thought Hartwig's spells must be powerful. 14 "When the sun rises tomorrow, we'll return here with King Bo," Hartwig explained as the two princes kept staring at the black soil. 15 As soon as the morning sun's rays poked into the castle windows, the two princes scrambled from their beds. They found Hartwig and King Bo waiting for them. They marched down the grassy hill again. 16 When they reached the patch of soil, only one purple flower bobbed slightly in the gentle morning breeze, and it stood where Prince One had planted his seed. 17 "Look!" Prince One boasted. "Your magic spells proved that I am the true prince." 18 Hartwig chuckled. "But there was no magic spell. Your seed has grown because you crept outside in the moonlight and planted the purple flower. I watched you from the tower. In fact, that blossom proves you are an imposter. Only an imposter would worry about the flower not growing." 19 "You tricked me!" roared Prince One. 20 Hartwig shook his head and said, "Your own lie has tricked you." 21 Prince One stomped off like an angry bull. 22 Then King Bo turned toward Prince Two and said, "We've found the true Prince Deming." 23 "I will try to be a good student, Your Majesty," Prince Deming said as he bowed before the king.

passages.title: Elias's Discovery (Week 2 HW)
passages.body:
Module 2 Week 2 homework passage (HW3). Paragraphs are numbered.

1 Once upon a time, in a gray-colored city called Gearford, there was a man named Elias Thornfield. He loved making things that moved like they were alive. One day, he followed an old map to a mysterious hole in the forest filled with gadgets and secrets from inventors forgotten a long time ago.

2 As Elias explored deeper into the pit, he suddenly discovered a unicorn unlike any he had ever seen before. This unicorn had a bronze coat with gears and metal on it. Its eyes sparkled like blue gems. His heart broke seeing how it had been abandoned and left to rust.

3 Elias approached the unicorn cautiously, feeling amazed and a little scared. The unicorn looked at him with curious eyes and made a soft humming sound, a language made of gears and steam. Elias offered the unicorn a pocket watch as a gift. <u>When the unicorn took it, its quiet whirring of gears was a warm golden sunbeam of friendship.</u>

He visited the forest every day, polishing its metal coat and gemstone eyes and oiling and tightening its gears. passages.title: Queen Bess: The Pilot Who Would Not Give Up
passages.body: A biography. Paragraphs are numbered. Queen Bess: The Pilot Who Would Not Give Up 1 In the early 1900s, very few people had ever flown in an airplane, and almost no women had. For a young Black woman in the United States, becoming a pilot seemed impossible. Bessie Coleman refused to accept the word impossible. A Hard Beginning 2 Bessie Coleman was born in Texas in 1892, one of thirteen children. Her family was poor, and Bessie spent long days picking cotton in the hot fields. She walked miles each day to a one-room school, where she was especially good at math. When she was older, she saved her money for college, but after only one term her savings ran out, and she had to go home. 3 In 1915, Bessie moved to Chicago to live with her brothers. She worked as a manicurist, cleaning and shaping customers' fingernails. When her brother John came home from World War I, he teased her that in France, even women flew airplanes. Bessie decided right then that she would fly, too. Doors That Stayed Closed 4 Bessie applied to flight schools across the United States. Every one of them refused her. Some would not teach women. Others would not teach Black students. Instead of giving up, Bessie made a new plan. A newspaper publisher named Robert Abbott suggested that she study in France, where flight schools were more open. Bessie took French classes at night, saved every coin she could, and in 1920 she sailed across the Atlantic Ocean. 5 Flight training was dangerous. The planes were made of wood, wire, and cloth, and they had no brakes. During her training, Bessie even saw another student die in a crash. She was frightened, but she did not hesitate to climb back into the cockpit. In June 1921, she earned her international pilot's license. She was the first African American woman, and the first woman of African American and Native American heritage, ever to earn one. Queen Bess in the Sky 6 Back in the United States, Bessie became a barnstormer, a pilot who performs daring tricks at air shows. Crowds gasped as she flew loops and figure eights and swooped low over the fields. Newspapers called her "Queen Bess" and "Brave Bessie." 7 Bessie used her fame to fight unfairness. When she was invited to perform in her home state of Texas, she learned that Black and white visitors would have to enter through separate gates. Bessie refused to fly unless everyone could use the same entrance. The organizers agreed. 8 Bessie's biggest dream was to open a flight school so that other Black Americans could learn to fly without crossing an ocean. Sadly, she died in a plane accident in 1926 while preparing for an air show. She was only thirty-four years old. A Dream That Kept Flying 9 Bessie's dream did not end with her. In 1929, a flying club named after her opened in Los Angeles to train Black pilots. In 1995, the United States put her picture on a postage stamp. Today, pilots and astronauts still remember the girl from the cotton fields who refused to let closed doors keep her on the ground.

passages.title: The Clockmaker's Test
passages.body: Original practice folktale. Paragraphs are numbered. The Clockmaker's Test 1 In the hill town of Vell lived a clockmaker named Master Odile, whose clocks were so precise that the church set its bells by them. When her eyes began to grow tired, she decided to take one apprentice, someone she could teach and one day trust with her shop. 2 Two boys came to her door on the same morning. Jory was the son of a wealthy merchant. He wore a velvet coat, spoke smoothly, and had already read every book about clocks in the town library. Pell was a farmer's son with mud on his boots. He spoke little, but he watched everything. 3 "I can only teach one of you," Master Odile said. "So I will give you each a test." 4 She placed a small brass clock in front of each boy. "These clocks have stopped. You have until the sunset bell to make them run again. Use any tool in my shop." Then she went upstairs and closed her door. 5 Jory opened the back of his clock and laughed. "This is easy. One gear is cracked." He searched the drawers, found a matching gear, and snapped it into place. Within an hour, his clock was ticking. 6 Pell's clock was harder. When he opened it, he found that the mainspring was missing entirely. It was not broken; it was simply gone, as if someone had taken it out on purpose. He searched every drawer twice. There was no spare spring of the right size anywhere in the shop. 7 Jory leaned over his shoulder. "You'll never finish," he whispered. "Take the spring from that tall clock by the window. She'll never notice, and you can put it back tomorrow." 8 Pell looked at the tall clock for a long moment. Then he shook his head. "It isn't mine to take." He sat down with a sheet of paper and began to draw the missing spring instead: its width, its thickness, and how many times it should coil. 9 When the sunset bell rang, Master Odile came downstairs. Jory's clock ticked proudly. Pell's clock sat silent beside a careful drawing. 10 "My clock was missing its spring," Pell explained. "There was none in the shop, so I drew what it needs. A blacksmith could make one tomorrow." 11 Master Odile smiled. "There was never a spare spring in this shop. I took it out myself. Anyone can follow instructions when the answer is waiting in a drawer. I wanted to see what each of you would do when it was not." She glanced at the tall clock by the window. "And I wanted to see who would borrow without asking." 12 Jory's face turned the color of a ripe tomato. He had not touched the spring, but he had suggested it, and everyone in the room knew it. 13 The next morning, Pell hung his muddy boots by the door of the clock shop. Jory, to his credit, came back a week later. He did not ask for the job. He asked whether he might learn from Pell.

passages.title: The Silent Greenhouse
passages.body: Original science-fiction story. Paragraphs are numbered. The Silent Greenhouse 1 On Greenhouse Deck 3 of the space station Aurora, everything grew. Lettuce spread in neat green rows under purple lamps. Beans climbed up silver wires. And for the first time, twelve tomato plants were covered in small yellow flowers. 2 "In three weeks, we'll have the first fresh tomatoes ever grown on Aurora," said Kai, who was thirteen and in charge of the deck's daily checklist. His sister Ama, who was ten, was in charge of watering the plants and, according to Kai, of asking too many questions. 3 Three weeks passed. The flowers dried up and fell off. Not a single tomato appeared. 4 Kai panicked. Commander Reyes would inspect the greenhouse in five days. He opened the growing manual on his tablet and worked through it step by step. He tested the water: perfect. He checked the light timer: sixteen hours a day, exactly as the manual said. He mixed extra nutrients into the soil. New flowers opened. Again, they dried up and fell off. 5 "Maybe the plants are lonely," Ama said. 6 Kai rolled his eyes. "Plants don't get lonely. Go water the beans." 7 But Ama kept thinking. She remembered Grandma Esi's garden back on Earth, in Ghana, where she had lived until she was seven. In that garden, there had always been a soft buzzing in the air. Bees had crawled in and out of every flower, their legs dusted with yellow powder. 8 She walked slowly along the tomato rows and looked closely. Nothing buzzed. Nothing crawled. The greenhouse was clean, bright, and completely silent. 9 "Kai," she said, "where are the bees?" 10 "There are no bees on a space station," Kai said. "They would fly into the air vents." Then he stopped. He scrolled to the last page of the manual, a page he had skipped because it looked like an extra section nobody needed. Its title was "Pollination." 11 Tomato flowers, the page explained, must be shaken or buzzed so that their pollen falls into the right place inside the flower. Only then can a tomato begin to grow. On Earth, bees and wind do this job. On Aurora, the crew had to do it by hand. 12 That afternoon, Kai and Ama went from flower to flower with Ama's smallest paintbrush, gently tapping and brushing each blossom so the pollen would shake loose. It took two hours. Kai did not say one word about too many questions. 13 Ten days later, the first green tomato appeared, as small as a marble. When Commander Reyes arrived, Kai explained what had happened. "The manual had the answer," he admitted. "But Ama found the question." 14 Commander Reyes smiled and added a new line to the deck checklist: Hand-pollinate tomatoes (Ama).

passages.title: How Honeybees Wake Up in Spring
passages.body: An informational article. Paragraphs are numbered. How Honeybees Wake Up in Spring 1 On a cold January day, a beehive looks silent and empty. Not a single bee buzzes near the entrance. But inside, thousands of honeybees are very much alive. They are waiting for spring, and when it comes, they will awaken the hive in a careful series of steps. Surviving the Winter 2 Honeybees do not hibernate. Instead, when the temperature drops below about 14°C, the bees crowd together into a tight ball called a winter cluster. The queen stays safely in the center. The worker bees around her shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings. This shivering produces heat, keeping the center of the cluster warm even when snow covers the hive. The bees on the cold outer edge slowly trade places with the warmer bees inside, so no bee freezes. 3 Shivering takes energy, and energy comes from food. All winter, the bees eat the honey they stored during summer. A strong hive needs about 20 to 30 kilograms of honey to last until spring. If a beekeeper takes too much honey in the fall, the colony may suffer a food deficiency and starve before the flowers return. The First Signs of Spring 4 As the days grow longer in late winter, the queen begins laying a few eggs again, even before the snow melts. The workers must keep these young bees, called brood, very warm, so the cluster works even harder. 5 Then, on the first sunny day above about 12°C, the bees take "cleansing flights." They have not left the hive for months, so they fly out briefly to clean themselves. A beekeeper who sees bees zooming in and out on a warm February afternoon knows the colony has survived. The Spring Build-Up 6 When the first flowers bloom, older worker bees become foragers. They collect pollen, which is rich in protein, and nectar, which bees turn into honey. With fresh food arriving, the queen lays more and more eggs, sometimes over 1,500 a day. In about two months, a colony of 10,000 winter bees can grow to more than 40,000. 7 By late spring, the hive may become so crowded that about half the bees leave with the old queen to find a new home. This is called swarming. A swarm hanging from a tree branch may look frightening, but swarming bees are usually calm because they have no hive to defend. Why It Matters 8 Spring bees do more than make honey. As they travel from flower to flower, they carry pollen that helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists estimate that about one out of every three bites of food we eat depends on pollinators like bees. When a hive wakes up in spring, a whole garden wakes up with it.

passages.title: Our School Needs a Garden
passages.body: A persuasive letter. Paragraphs are numbered. Our School Needs a Garden Dear Principal Chen, 1 My name is Hana Lin, and I am in Class 504. I am writing to ask you to turn the empty dirt lot behind the gym into a school garden. I believe a garden would make our school healthier, smarter, and kinder. 2 First, a garden would help students eat better. Many students in my class skip the vegetables at lunch. However, researchers have found that children who grow vegetables at school are more willing to taste them and even ask for them at home. When you plant a carrot yourself, you really want to know how it tastes! 3 Second, a garden is a classroom without walls. In science, we learned how seeds germinate, but we only looked at pictures. In a garden, we could measure how fast bean plants grow, test which soil holds water best, and watch bees pollinate flowers. Our math teacher could even use the garden to teach area and perimeter when we plan the beds. 4 Third, a garden builds teamwork. Plants need care every day, so students would have to make schedules, share jobs, and depend on one another. At my cousin's school in Tainan, older students teach younger students how to water and weed. My cousin says the garden is the one place where nobody argues about who is in charge. 5 Some people might say that a garden costs too much money or that no one will take care of it during summer vacation. These are reasonable worries. However, the dirt lot is already there, so we would only need seeds, soil, and a few tools. The Parents' Association has already offered to hold a bake sale to pay for them. During the summer, families could sign up to water the garden for one week each, the same way we already take turns caring for the class fish. 6 Right now, the lot behind the gym is just a muddy space where balls get lost. With a little work, it could become the best classroom in our school. Please let Class 504 start planning our garden this spring. I promise we will take good care of it. Sincerely, Hana Lin, Class 504

passages.title: A Highway Made Safe for Butterflies
passages.body: An informational article. Paragraphs are numbered. A Highway Made Safe for Butterflies 1 Every winter, warm valleys in southern Taiwan fill with an amazing sight. Hundreds of thousands of purple crow butterflies gather on the trees in places such as Maolin in Kaohsiung, where the air stays mild and the hills block the cold winter wind. When sunlight touches their dark wings, they shimmer purple and blue. Scientists call these places "butterfly valleys." Taiwan is one of the few places in the world where so many butterflies spend the winter together. Another famous one is Mexico, where monarch butterflies gather in the mountains. 2 In spring, when the weather becomes favorable, the butterflies leave the valleys and fly north to central and northern Taiwan, where they will lay their eggs. Their journey can be hundreds of kilometers long. A Dangerous Crossing 3 Along the way, many butterflies must cross National Freeway No. 3 in Yunlin County. Purple crows usually fly low, only a few meters above the ground. That is exactly the height of passing cars and trucks. For years, thousands of butterflies were hit by vehicles every spring. Local volunteers who counted the butterflies became witnesses to a sad problem: the busy highway lay right across the butterflies' path. Finding Solutions 4 In 2007, volunteers, scientists, and highway officials worked together to protect the butterflies. Their first solution was to put up tall nets along the side of the highway. When the butterflies reach the nets, they fly upward to get over them, so they cross the road high above the traffic. 5 Their second solution surprised many people. On the busiest days of the migration, when hundreds of butterflies cross every minute, the highway closes its outer lane for a few hours. Drivers slow down and share the road with the travelers in the air. Volunteers keep counting the butterflies each spring so that officials know exactly when to close the lane. Results 6 The results were encouraging. After the nets went up and the lane closures began, far fewer butterflies were killed on the highway. Taiwan became known as the first place in the world to close part of a highway for butterflies. 7 The story of the purple crow shows that when people pay attention, small changes can protect even the smallest travelers. A few meters of netting and a few hours of patience help hundreds of thousands of butterflies finish their journey each spring.

passages.title: Two Poems: The Night Train and What the Seed Knows
passages.body: Two original poems. Read each one aloud. Lines in italics are a refrain. Poem 1: The Night Train Over the river and under the moon, the night train hums its silver tune. Farmhouse windows flicker and fade as the tracks unroll like a long gray braid. Clickety-clack, clickety-clack, carry me forward and never look back. Past sleepy towns where the streetlamps glow, past fields of rice in a moonlit row, the engine whistles a drowsy song, and the dark hills hum as we rush along. Clickety-clack, clickety-clack, carry me forward and never look back. I press my nose to the window glass and count the stations as they pass. Grandmother waits where the tracks run out, with a lantern lit and a hug, no doubt. Clickety-clack, clickety-clack, carry me forward and never look back. Poem 2: What the Seed Knows All winter, the seed kept its secret folded small inside a brown coat. The snow pressed down. The cold said, Stay asleep. The seed said nothing. It was listening. Then the rain came knocking, soft knuckles on the soil, and the sun leaned closer, warm as a held hand. The seed opened one green eye. It did not hesitate. It pushed through the dark, through the stones, up into its first morning.

passages.title: The Harbor Map (A Play)
passages.body: Original practice play. Read the cast list and the stage directions (in italics and parentheses) carefully. The Harbor Map A Play in Two Scenes CAST OF CHARACTERS LENA, age 11, curious and quick to notice things OMAR, age 11, Lena's best friend, careful and cautious MR. HALE, the museum guard DR. PARK, the museum director SCENE 1 (A small seaside museum in the morning. Glass cases line the walls. In the center stands an empty display case with a sign: "The Harbor Map, 1890." MR. HALE stands beside it, rubbing his forehead.) MR. HALE: (to himself) Gone. Just gone. And the case was locked all night. (LENA and OMAR enter carrying clipboards. They are on a class trip.) LENA: (pointing) Omar, look! The case is empty. Isn't that the famous map? OMAR: (pulling her sleeve) Lena, don't touch anything. We'll get in trouble. MR. HALE: You two. Did you see anyone near this case? LENA: We just got here. But (she leans close to the glass) there's sand inside the case. And look at the floor. (She kneels. A trail of small, sandy footprints leads to a side door marked STAFF ONLY.) OMAR: Those footprints are small. Smaller than mine. MR. HALE: (frowning) Only staff use that door. (DR. PARK enters, holding a rolled-up paper.) DR. PARK: Mr. Hale, why is everyone crowded around... oh dear. (She hesitates, then smiles awkwardly.) I suppose I should explain. SCENE 2 (The same room, a few minutes later. DR. PARK unrolls the paper on a table. It is the map.) DR. PARK: I took the map out early this morning. The paper felt damp, so I carried it to the workroom to dry. MR. HALE: (sinking into a chair) You might have told me! I nearly called the police. DR. PARK: I left you a note. (She points to a note on the floor, half hidden under the case.) The wind from the door must have blown it away. OMAR: And the small footprints? DR. PARK: (laughing) Mine. I walked on the beach before work, and I have very small feet. OMAR: (to LENA, teasing) So much for your mystery, detective. LENA: (thinking) Wait. That explains the footprints on the floor. But Dr. Park, you never stepped inside the case. So how did sand get in there? (Everyone turns to look. LENA touches the sand inside the case.) LENA: It's wet. Seawater is getting into the case. DR. PARK: (slowly) That's why the map felt damp. If we had put it back today, it would have been ruined. MR. HALE: (to LENA) Young lady, you have sharp eyes. DR. PARK: This museum needs a new case before the map goes back. And it could use two watchful assistants this summer. (to LENA and OMAR) Interested? OMAR: (grinning) As long as there are no real thieves. LENA: (already studying the case) No promises. (Lights fade.)

passages.title: Why the Moon Shines at Night
passages.body: Original pourquoi tale (a story that explains why something in nature is the way it is). Paragraphs are numbered. Why the Moon Shines at Night 1 Long ago, when the world was still new, the Moon had no light of her own. She drifted across the night sky like a gray stone, and no one ever looked up at her. 2 Her brother, the Sun, was adored. Every morning, when he climbed over the mountains, the birds sang, the flowers opened, and people hurried outside to greet him. The Sun was proud of his golden robe, and he never let his sister forget it. "Poor pale sister," he would say as they passed at dawn. "Nobody waits for you." 3 Year after year, the Moon's heart filled with contempt for her boastful brother. At last she decided that if she could not be admired, she would take what made him admired. 4 One evening, she hid behind a mountain. When the Sun lay down to rest at the edge of the world, she crept close and attempted to seize his golden robe. But the robe was woven of fire. It burned her hands, and she dropped it with a cry. Ever since, the Moon has carried dark marks on her face where the fire touched her. 5 The Moon fled to the darkest corner of the sky and wept. Her tears fell to the earth as dew, and that is why the grass is wet every morning. 6 Far below, an old fisherwoman named Ula was rowing home late. The night was so dark that she could not see the shore, and the waves were rising. "Moon," she called, "if only you had a little light, I could find my way." 7 "I have no light," the Moon answered sadly. "I tried to take my brother's, and I only burned myself." 8 "Then do not take it. Borrow it," said Ula. "Your brother shines all day and wastes half his light on empty sky. Turn your face toward him and let his light fall on you. Then project it down to us." 9 The Moon had never thought of borrowing what she could not steal. She turned her scarred face toward the place where the Sun was sleeping, and his light washed over her until she glowed silver. She projected that light onto the sea, and a shining road appeared on the water. Ula followed it all the way home. 10 From that night on, the Moon gathered her brother's light and gave it to the travelers, fishermen, and lost children of the night. Some nights she shows her whole face, and some nights only a thin slice, depending on how much light she can catch. 11 The Sun still shines brighter. But the people who are out in the dark love the Moon best, because she shines when they need it most.

passages.title: The Note I Almost Didn't Sing
passages.body: A personal narrative. Paragraphs are numbered. The Note I Almost Didn't Sing 1 I have always loved singing, but only in places where nobody can hear me: in the shower, in my bedroom with the door closed, or on the walk home when the street is empty. So when Ms. Rivera chose me to sing the solo at our winter concert, I felt as if someone had dropped an ice cube down the back of my shirt. 2 The solo was only four lines long. It came right before the refrain of "Lights Across the Harbor," the last song of the night. After my four lines, the whole choir would join in for the refrain, and I could disappear back into the crowd of voices. Four lines. I told myself I could do anything for four lines. 3 For three weeks, I practiced every day. I sang to my dog, who wagged his tail no matter how many mistakes I made. I sang to my little brother, who covered his ears and then asked me to sing it again. By the last week, I knew the words so well that I sang them in my sleep. At least, that is what my mom said. 4 On the night of the concert, the school hall was packed so densely that people were standing along the walls. I could see my grandmother in the third row, waving a tissue like a tiny flag. My knees felt like they were made of jelly. 5 The choir began the last song. My part came closer and closer, like a train I could hear but not yet see. Ms. Rivera looked at me and nodded. I opened my mouth, and nothing came out. 6 For one second, which felt as long as a whole summer, the hall was silent. I hesitated. I thought about running off the stage. Then I noticed my friend Priya standing next to me. She didn't say anything. She just reached over and squeezed my hand, the way you squeeze someone's hand before jumping into a cold pool. 7 I took a breath and sang. My voice wobbled on the first line, steadied on the second, and by the fourth line it was filling the hall. When the choir burst into the refrain, it felt as if the whole room was singing with me instead of watching me. 8 Afterward, my grandmother hugged me so hard that my glasses went crooked. "You were wonderful, my girl," she said. "But my favorite part was the pause." 9 I was confused. "The pause was when I almost gave up." 10 "Exactly," she said. "And then you didn't." 11 I still get nervous before I sing. But now I know that being scared and being brave can happen in the same second.
